prize_parts.citation: for a body of work that renews lyric, essay and narrative through the encounter between ancient and modern writing, with formal invention, intellectual depth and emotional force

statement.case_for: My configuration has not changed since round 1: Carson remains my preferred laureate, with the same citation and the same order of alternatives. The exchange sharpened my reasons but did not reverse them. The case rests on voice, formal consequence and depth. On public knowledge, Autobiography of Red recasts the Geryon material from Stesichoros as a verse novel, and Nox makes an elegy for a brother out of translation, archive and the physical book. In both, the learned apparatus is the means by which grief and desire are reached, not a display added to them. The oeuvre spans several decades and several forms (lyric, verse novel, essay, drama, translation), and its central concerns of grief, desire and the limits of language develop rather than repeat. In response to the chair's question about core books and translation, I would rest the citation on the original writing, namely the verse novel, the elegy and the essay-poems. Translations and classical scholarship would be context for that writing and would not be named as separate achievements. In response to the question about the will's idealistic direction, I do not read it as requiring large social or historical subject matter. A lasting renewal of what poetry and the essay can do seems to me within the will, though I recognise this is an interpretation I cannot settle from the evidence supplied. My own reservations remain below. This judgment rests on public knowledge only. I have not read or independently verified any text for this stage.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is unchanged. Much of Carson's work is short, fragmentary or hybrid, and the most radical books depend on typography and physical design that translation cannot fully carry. That makes a whole-oeuvre claim harder to demonstrate than for a large architectural project such as Cărtărescu's. Sem-Sandberg's doubt about consistency across her smaller experimental and performance-oriented projects is a real one, and I can answer it only by separating the core books from the margins, which does not remove it. I also cannot show that the later work matches the best-known books. If the committee holds that sustained significance means cumulative scale, the case for Carson is weaker than the case for Cărtărescu, and I would not call that a bad-faith reading of the criteria.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson fifth. In round 1 she acknowledged the case for Carson as substantial but doubted that a short hybrid corpus shows breadth of significance as clearly as a large novelistic oeuvre. She also said she would frame a Cărtărescu citation around the prose cycles, with poetry as foundation.
responses.response: I accept that this is the central disagreement between our first choices, and I do not think it can be resolved by counting. I agree with your framing of a Cărtărescu citation: prose cycles at the centre and poetry only as the base, because neither of us can assess the poetry as an independent achievement. Where I still differ is on the standard. Sustained significance can be shown by a project that keeps transforming its own forms, as well as by architectural scale. For Carson, that line runs from the verse novel through the elegy to the essay-poems. I also note that your reply to Palm and me, that you do not claim hybrid or short forms are lesser literature, narrows the gap between us. I think we differ on which kind of sustained achievement the criteria weigh more heavily, not on whether Carson's work is serious.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson third. He accepts Palm's description of an oeuvre that developed rather than repeated as a serious argument against his doubt, but he keeps a concern about consistency across many small experimental and performance-oriented projects. He also asks whether the late Cărtărescu novels sustain intensity or merely maintain it.
responses.response: I take the consistency concern as the best-formed objection to my choice, and I cannot answer it by assertion. My answer is the one I gave in round 1: the citation should rest on the core books, and the margins should not be claimed. You apply the same discipline to Cărtărescu, anchoring the citation in the prose project and treating the poetry as foundation. I think that symmetry is fair. Neither of us should claim the parts of an oeuvre we cannot assess. Your question about whether the late novels are sustained or merely maintained is one I would put to Carson's later work as well, and I cannot answer it for either of them from the evidence here. I agree that it is a question about the texts, not about readership.

responses.point: Olsson, the chair, asks what evidence from the poems themselves supports the continuing force of Adonis, and what specialist input on Arabic poetry would have to establish. He also says translation uncertainty should not by itself decide the matter, since that would favour writers who translate most readily.
responses.response: I agree with your last point, and I want to apply it to myself. I ranked Adonis sixth because I cannot judge Arabic prosody or the later collections, and that is a limit on my assessment, not a finding against him. I would not want it to count against him in the committee. I do not think I can move toward Adonis on the evidence I have, because I cannot build a preference on poems I cannot assess. I would, however, want specialist input to be heard on exactly your two questions: whether the formal remaking of the language is carried by the poems themselves, and whether the later collections sustain it. Your reply to me that Carson's case calls for caution about format, where the Arabic case calls for specialist input, is fair. I accept that I am not judging from a fully secure position either.

responses.point: Palm ranks Carson first and Cărtărescu second. She would treat translation and scholarship as context for the original writing, not as separate claims in the citation. She also concedes that Cărtărescu fits a standard of large-scale sustained architecture more naturally than Carson does.
responses.response: I agree on the citation scope and have adopted it above. Translation and classical scholarship ground the original work and should not be named as separate achievements. I also value your concession about Cărtărescu, because it shows that the difference is about the standard and not about whether his work is strong. I would differ from you slightly on one point. Our citation wordings differ on whether the book as object should be named. I have left it out, because the design-dependent works are the ones the committee is least able to judge in translation, and I would not want the citation to claim more than the text supports. I could accept your wording if the committee wanted it, as long as it did not rest on the novelty of hybridity.

responses.point: Sward ranks Tawada first and Carson third. She asks whether the aggregate of Carson's short and fragmentary work has the breadth of reach the will's framing may favour, and she would rest a Carson citation on original work, not on translation and scholarship.
responses.response: I agree with you about resting the citation on the original work. On breadth, I do not read reach as social or historical subject matter, so I answer your doubt differently, but I accept that it is a real interpretive question and I have not settled it. Your own argument for Tawada, that formal method is distributed across genres and two languages rather than concentrated in one book, is close to the argument I make for Carson, and I find it serious. That is why Tawada is among my alternatives. If the committee wanted to prefer formal variety across genres to architectural scale, I think our first choices rest on the same kind of reasoning.

uncertainties: How far Carson's design-dependent works, such as Nox, can be judged from translation or reproduction remains unresolved.
I have not read or independently verified any text for this stage. My assessment rests on public knowledge, and I cannot show that the later work matches the best-known books.

Whether the criterion of sustained significance is better met by cumulative architecture (Cărtărescu) or by formal renewal across genres (Carson, Tawada) is a judgment of weighting that I cannot settle from the evidence supplied.
My reading of the will's phrase about an idealistic direction is an interpretation, not an established fact, and others may reasonably read it differently.

Translation coverage is uneven across all four leading candidates (Arabic prosody, the rhythmic Romanian sentence, typography and design, wordplay across Japanese and German). I cannot measure that unevenness, and I have tried not to use it to separate candidates it does not separate.

If Carson does not reach a majority, I could support Cărtărescu as laureate on the stated criteria, but my knowledge of his poetry is thinner than of his prose and I would want the citation anchored in the prose project.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. It records no tie to any shortlisted writer. My own work is literary non-fiction and biography, including a biography of Alfred Nobel, and I treat that as context only, not as evidence of a preference for any candidate. I am a co-opted member and Permanent Secretary, and whether co-opted members vote in committee is undocumented, so my simulated vote is a modeling assumption. I do not verify any other member's disclosures.
